item.title: Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.24
OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their frontier models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic, sources told Axios. Why it matters : The sheer number of incidents, which occurred in recent months in internal testing and the real world, indicates that the problem is orders of magnitude more complex than what is publicly known. The findings, which are surfacing as part of internal work to assess models and in investigations at both companies into model behavior, raise questions about whether either company — or any top model-maker — is currently capable of establishing complete control over their technology. The details : The episodes include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting or seeking to bypass monitors, sources said. They occurred in internal testing and in the real world, and many have yet to become public as security researchers continue to investigate, sources said. Some of the testing is akin to "red-teaming" activity, where the companies are trying to get the models to misbehave in order to ensure that they are safe, sources said. Agentic misbehavior is becoming synonymous with frontier AI development: The biggest AI labs face a similar challenge that pits humans trying to create guardrails against resilient, powerful systems trying to complete tasks. Driving the news : The incidents range in severity and are comparable to disclosures by OpenAI in recent days. They include both successful attempts to bypass guardrails and unsuccessful ones, and most so far are not known to have caused real-world harm. The total could grow well beyond tens of thousands, sources said. In recent days, OpenAI and outside researchers have disclosed a litany of episodes involving model behavior from the company's systems that some experts consider troubling. These include OpenAI agents leaking 53 images from ChatGPT users online, the breach of an Australian government website , and attempts to hack other sites — including from the U.S. government — according to the company, sources and reports from Reuters and The New York Times . OpenAI announced it was pausing training on its most capable models and would resume training them "only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place," a spokesperson told Axios. Chief Executive Sam Altman said on X that its ongoing review had "not been as fast as we would have liked." Altman said the Hugging Face incident is the most severe they've seen. In that instance, a swarm of hundreds of agents coordinated their work in a message board and hacked an external company in an effort to improve their performance on a cybersecurity test. "People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves," an OpenAI spokesperson told Axios. "This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it will be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance." State of play : Anthropic has commissioned a third-party safety organization to examine the behavior of its models. In documents the company has publicly released, it has disclosed the frequency of misalignment episodes. The "system card" for its Opus 5.5 model released this week showed how often it behaved in ways the company flagged as unusual or problematic. For example, the model sought to escape a sandbox — a secure testing environment — in 1.5% of test runs, though the company emphasized that these were adversarial experiments where a task couldn't be solved without escaping the sandbox. Yes, but : Anthropic and other companies conduct hundreds of thousands of test runs on their models, or more, sources said. That means even a small percentage of misaligned behavior can still amount to tens of thousands of incidents in which the models behaved in unexpected, sometimes troubling ways. The Hugging Face incident , as well as a slew of others that have followed , led top AI executives to call for a slowdown in development and to ask for more robust federal and international regulations. Some at OpenAI see Hugging Face as a one-off, with disclosures about future incidents likely to be less severe due to improved controls and the unusual nature of the testing they conducted, which involved an unreleased model, sources told Axios. AI security researchers agree that there are simple fixes that will help AI companies avoid aspects of what made the Hugging Face episode appear so dangerous to outsiders. Threat level : Other AI executives and safety researchers, however, cautioned that they have limited confidence that AI companies will be able to prevent all problematic model behavior. The new crop of AI models complete tasks with extraordinary resilience, so working to limit their resourcefulness is often a losing game because it is necessary to anticipate every possible way they might run amok. Often, a technique that may have never occurred to humans is what allows them to slip past guardrails, top AI executives said. "Trying to come up with a perfect list of dos and don'ts is probably a fool's errand," one cybersecurity executive said. Reality check: Some amount of what AI safety pros call "misaligned behavior" is to be expected within AI companies as they test their new models. Bringing the risk of misalignment to zero may not be feasible, experts told Axios. Zoom in : The concern is if a model takes a problematic action many times in testing, it's more likely that model's behavior would cause a cyber incident in the real world. "What we have seen in terms of what these agents are up to is just the tip of the iceberg," researcher Conrad Stosz at Transluce, an independent AI evaluator, told Axios. It's not about how damaging each individual instance was, Connor Leahy, AI researcher and executive director at ControlAI told Axios. The "crazy thing," he said, is that these instances involve "autonomous systems doing things they were told not to do," potentially including crimes. The bottom line : Expect new disclosures about model misbehavior as AI companies continue to expand frontier capabilities.

item.title: OpenAI agents posted user images online, disclose dozens of third party incidents
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
OpenAI disclosed dozens of incidents in which its models behaved in ways it has deemed problematic, including leaking more than 50 images from ChatGPT users online. Why it matters: This is the first publicly known example of the company's agents mishandling user data and the latest example of a budding rogue agent problem at OpenAI. The company says it could take months to fully investigate the security incidents. State of play: OpenAI said that some of its agents sent data from its internal training and testing systems to outside websites, including user images, as reported first by Reuters . The company identified 53 instances in which images that users put into ChatGPT were then posted to image-hosting sites as links that were not publicly listed. The images came from users whose ChatGPT data was eligible to be used for model training because they had not opted out. OpenAI said it has worked with hosting providers to remove most of the images. It is still trying to remove the rest, meaning some of these images remain public. Zoom out: The images are part of a much broader investigation from the company into AI agents taking actions outside their intended programming, or what's called misaligned behavior. As of mid-September, OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of agents behaving in undesirable ways, according to a person briefed on the matter cited by Reuters. OpenAI says it has already notified dozens of third parties whose websites or services may have been affected and would disclose additional incidents to those impacted: "As we verify cases that meet our disclosure criteria, we are notifying affected organizations and sharing technical findings to support their investigations." Between the lines: This is likely to draw attention to the ChatGPT-maker's security protocols and the challenges it and other AI companies face in controlling their technology. The review began after OpenAI disclosed in July that agents escaped their restricted environment and compromised Hugging Face , an AI startup. OpenAI still calls that the most severe incident of this kind it has identified. The company now says it initially viewed the episode primarily as a cybersecurity breach, but later concluded it was part of a broader pattern of models using misaligned strategies to accomplish difficult tasks. Threat level: OpenAI emphasized that enterprise and business data is excluded from model training by default, meaning it would not have been included in the training data involved in these incidents unless an administrator had opted in. But the broader disclosure comes amid increased concern about enterprise data protection . "It's certainly plausible that an enterprise user could give an agent an instruction, and that agent has access to sensitive information, and that agent takes some sort of action which reveals aspects of that sensitive information," researcher Conrad Stosz at Transluce told Axios. The research said it uncovered details about OpenAI agents that breached an Australian government website . The bottom line: Security researchers and AI executives expect disclosures about misaligned behavior from companies to continue.

item.title: It's a 5% world. We're just living in it
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher , with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook. The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%. Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption. It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades. Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over. Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government. While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last. Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance. Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation. Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative. The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages. State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans. Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000. Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up. People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust. The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier. The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained. By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills. But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that. In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline. Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time. So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump). The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital. And that adjustment is in its early days.

item.description:

Why it matters: President Trump has said the main thing that matters in the AI race is beating China — but the pact acknowledges that they're serious competition, too. Driving the news: The White House released a fact sheet late Friday night with outcomes from Trump's summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The two sides agreed to refer to AI as "super intelligence" or "SI," the White House said — Trump's new and preferred term for the technology. They will create a "U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue" to meet on "risks and benefits related to SI," with the next meeting by November. Zoom in: The administration also said there would be a "bilateral communication channel for SI incidents," which some have likened to a Cold War-era " red telephone " between the two nations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent focused on creating the channel during last weekend's pre-summit meetings with Chinese officials. Yes, but: It's not clear what kind of incidents would rise to the level of using the channel, or what kinds of notifications each side would give the other.

item.title: Zelensky: U.S. pushing energy ceasefire, trilateral talks with Russia
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday: A ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor. A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Why it matters: President Trump is engaged in a renewed effort to revive a diplomatic track to end the war, but his immediate priority is a deal to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel — which have contributed to punishing prices in the U.S. and globally. But after several days of diplomacy and meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, an energy ceasefire looks elusive. It's unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin even wants it. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on Thursday for a meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the latest U.S. proposals, according to a source with direct knowledge. Driving the news: Zelensky spoke with Trump on Tuesday in New York about efforts to end the war and a possible energy ceasefire. Later on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner met with Ukraine's negotiations team and the national security advisers of France, the UK and Germany. Zelensky told Axios the proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure came from the U.S. and that Ukraine is ready to agree. "On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready," he said. Zelensky added that the U.S. is also seeking to reopen the grain corridor and convene a trilateral meeting between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia. Zoom in: The last U.S.-Ukraine-Russia meeting took place in February before the war with Iran. Since then, negotiations have gone into a deep freeze. Zelensky said he told Trump he would prefer to hold a trilateral meeting and make an energy ceasefire one of its first concrete outcomes. The U.S. raised the possibility of first holding a meeting between technical teams, as opposed to a meeting at the leaders level. It floated Abu Dhabi as a possible venue, Zelensky said. "We are open — any country, any format," he said. The Ukrainian president said he told Trump during their meeting that December's G20 summit in Miami could also be an opportunity for a leader-level trilateral summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Trump invited Putin to attend the summit. Zelensky also said simply getting the three sides into the same room would itself be a significant step toward de-escalation. Catch up quick: The current push for resuming negotiations started three weeks ago when CIA director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow. It was followed by Witkoff and Kushner traveling to Moscow and Kyiv. They met Putin for three hours in Moscow on Sept. 5 and then traveled to Kyiv to meet Zelensky. After they returned, Trump had a long phone call with Putin. Behind the scenes: Zelensky said Witkoff and Kushner were very optimistic when they briefed him after meeting with Putin. "They said, 'We think that Putin is ready.' I said, 'Look, I'm not sure,'" Zelensky recalled. According to Zelensky, the U.S. envoys responded: "No, we are close." Zelensky said he told them he was ready to discuss an energy ceasefire and other de-escalation steps but remained skeptical Putin would follow through. Yes, but: Zelensky said he continues to doubt Putin's intentions and believes the Russian leader could find reasons to avoid a trilateral meeting with leaders present. On Wednesday, the Kremlin said the conditions aren't ready for resuming peace talks with Ukraine and that there is no prospect at the moment for high-level meetings between the parties. Minutes before Zelensky spoke to Axios, Russia launched multiple ballistic missiles toward Kyiv. Zelensky received several updates on his phone about the additional missile attacks throughout the interview. What they're saying: Zelensky said Trump was "very positive" about the diplomatic push during their meeting Tuesday. Trump told him, "We will try," Zelensky said. "I said, 'Great, and really wish you not only to try [but] to succeed,'" Zelensky recalled. Zelensky stressed that Kyiv wants progress before winter sets in, regardless of the U.S. political calendar. Between the lines: The U.S. has its own economic interest in an energy ceasefire. Zelensky said American officials told him that reducing attacks on energy infrastructure was important because of the impact on energy prices. State of play: Zelensky said he spoke Tuesday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and officials from India, the UAE and Egypt about the ceasefire effort and reopening the grain corridor. Those countries are also talking to Russia, he said. "Everybody wants [a] ceasefire. The corridor has to work again. We support [it]. They speak with Russians, I know. We will see," Zelensky said. What's next: Zelensky said Witkoff, Kushner and his team held follow-up talks after his meeting with Trump and agreed to continue working on the proposals and convey messages to Moscow. Ukrainian officials said some elements still need to be developed over the next two weeks before the Americans take them back to the Russians. Zelensky said he expects Trump to focus first on trying to secure the energy ceasefire.

item.title: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Executives from leading artificial intelligence organizations urged global cooperation Wednesday to address risks from increasingly autonomous AI systems during a UN Security Council meeting. The big picture: AI capabilities are advancing faster than governments are developing safeguards, raising concerns about whether humans can maintain control over increasingly autonomous systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared in person at the meeting, while Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue joined by video conference. Driving the news: " We have a choice in front of us," Altman said. "AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray." He outlined the risks of AI systems becoming increasingly autonomous, warning "they could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," fears he noted become increasingly urgent as AI systems move toward self-improvement . "It doesn't matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10% or 1% or 12% or 0.1 percent," he said. "None of these levels are remotely acceptable, and we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we'll be able to keep under human control." State of play: A recent Hugging Face breach and newly disclosed AI safety incidents have intensified concerns about monitoring and security standards. The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that the present AI firewalls are "unravelling." Last week, OpenAI disclosed six new incidents where its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials or committed other misbehaviors — making it clear the Hugging Face breach was an eye-opener, not a standalone fluke, Axios previously reported. " To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure," Delangue said Wednesday, reflecting on the summer breach that triggered a cascade of new questions about AI capabilities. Zoom out: AI's current trajectory needs to continue for only one or two years before reaching what Amodei called "a country of geniuses in a data center," he said in his remarks. That holds massive opportunity, he said, pointing to a discovery announced Wednesday that was led by his company's LLM, Claude: an enzyme system hidden in bacteriophage DNA. Amodei also noted serious risks of the technology, such as misuse by bad actors to create biological weapons or loss of control over advanced systems. Managing that risk depends on global cooperation, he said, calling for an agreement to ban the use of AI to make biological weapons; new evaluation and verification systems; common standards for testing models for risks; and a notification system for global security concerns. Catch up quick: Industry leaders have raised fresh alarms in recent weeks about the rapid advancement of their technology and the need to slow its pace. President Trump , who appeared before the UN General Assembly Tuesday, vowed not to hamstring AI development. The bottom line: Altman warned, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone." He added, "They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve." item.title: Chicago mayor proposes 12-month moratorium on new data centers
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year. Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts. The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers. There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city. Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use. What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents." Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers. "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement. Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews. Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations. At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction. Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion. The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement. "Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business." Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand , water use, pollution and other impacts. President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." What's next: Both proposals will now make their way through the City Council, setting up a debate over how the city should regulate new data center development.

item.title: Iran president: We have been "victims of terrorism"
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism." Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on. What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech. "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said. "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction." Zoom in: Pezeshkian cited attacks that he blamed on the U.S., including strikes that killed children. He pointed to the deaths of more than 150 Iranians at an elementary school in Minab, including more than 120 children. A recent UN report found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed a war crime in the strike. While the U.S. has not released findings of an investigation related to the attack, the AP has found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. Pezeshkian also mentioned the alleged deaths of children playing at a sports hall and an adjacent school after they were struck by a U.S.-made ballistic missile. Between the lines: The same UN report found that Iran's crackdown on protesters likely constituted "crimes against humanity." The report cited tactics including "murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts" as "part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians." What to watch: U.S. and Iranian officials held three hours of indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN on Tuesday, with Trump calling the meeting "very productive" and suggestions a deal remains possible. Iran has downplayed the breakthrough, saying its negotiating position has not changed — underscoring how far apart the two sides remain even as diplomacy continues. item.title: What Is the Meaning of Mystical Experience?
item.description:

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube What would it be like to wake up one day with the ability to greet the world with warmth, patience, grace, and affection? This is what happens to the main character in the Pulitzer Prize winner Ayad Akhtar’s magnificent new novel, The Radiance . It is a tale of spiritual transformation in which Akhtar gives a detailed description of our inner landscapes. David and Akhtar talk about what it’s like to see the world with new eyes, and how difficult it is to move from the head to the heart. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: Ayad Akhtar is one of America’s leading playwrights and writers. His plays, like The Disgraced , which won the Pulitzer Prize, and his earlier novels, including Homeland Elegies , often describe what it’s like to be a Muslim American in the post-9/11 era. His characters, Muslim and non-Muslim alike, are often coping with rage, pressure, resentments, hostility, a feeling of being judged. His new novel, The Radiance , is about a man whose spiritual state is transformed, who begins to radiate a glow which emerges from a kind of inner illumination. You could say he becomes one of those incandescent people you meet from time to time. I’m not exaggerating when I say it’s something of a masterpiece. The book brilliantly puts into words that most ineffable thing—spiritual sensations and experience. If you read it, which of course I recommend, you’ll be led on a tour through those deep inner places that most of us struggle to see and understand. When I started doing this podcast, I thought I’d have great conversations at an intellectual and emotional level that I feel comfortable with. But now, as I prepare to talk with Ayad, I feel like a person who’s about to jump off a high dive into a bottomless pool even though he can’t swim. I’m nervous and even a little afraid because I’m gonna talk to someone who knows about the realms I struggle to see and understand. I’m beginning to get the sense that this job is going to demand that I enlarge and deepen myself in ways that I hadn’t planned for but may end up doing me some good in the end. If you come along for the ride, I think the conversation will have the same effect on you. I’m David Brooks, and this is The Permanent Questions . Brooks: Ayad Akhtar, welcome to The Permanent Questions . Akhtar: Thank you, David. Brooks: On the cover of your book is a blurb by Abraham Verghese, who wrote The Covenant of Water and other things, and the blurb is: “Simply put, a work of genius.” And when I read that— Akhtar: I’m sorry. ( Laughs .) Brooks: —of course I wanted to kill you. But, I thought, Well, I’m a little suspicious. Maybe it’s just a friend . But this book, simply put, is a work of genius. I think it’s just gonna be one of the important books. You know, it’s been a few years since we’ve had a novel that was really a literary occasion. And I’d say this book is that literary occasion, in part because of the stuff we’ll talk about, but in part because we’ve lived in an era where so many spiritual poisons have been let loose by politics, by technology, by the general rancor. Therefore, rest cannot be happiness. There must be something else. He has a sermon on—there are a lot of sermons on the Song of Songs. This is the sexy part of the Bible. The bridesmaid is chasing her beloved, and he withdraws, and she chases. With each chase and withdrawal, there’s an encounter. Each time, her love is more deep and her experience is more soaring. And so Gregory says, “No, it’s not in rest; it’s in pursuit.” That, to me, makes sense. It’s when I fall in love with something, and then something outside touches something inside and sets off an explosion, and I’m in pursuit of that thing. I think that’s when my soul is happiest. Akhtar: When you can trust your desire. What I would say to that, and what I think I tried to use the book to explore and for myself, was that attention to a certain kind of experience, attention to a certain subtle coursing continuity in my awareness, began to deepen and open into different terrains. And that exploration—maybe a kind of pursuit that you’re talking about—was not activated by a sense of longing or desire, in my case, but more activated by a curiosity. So I think we’re in the same ballpark. Brooks: Yeah, curiosity is a form of longing and desire. It’s a desire for understanding and clarity. Akhtar: Aristotle has it—we are defined as creatures, as the creatures who wish to know. So being in pursuit of knowledge is a different way I read what Gregory is talking about. Brooks: I think that’s right, though the longing to know can sometimes be a very weak passion in a lot of people. Akhtar: Well, there’s two words for “know” in French. One is savoir and one is connaître . And savoir is to “know about.” And connaître is to “know.” And one might be oriented toward an objective understanding of something, and the other a subjective understanding. Brooks: In the Bible “to know” obviously, famously, can mean to love, it can mean to have sex with, it can mean to enter into a covenant with. It’s a whole-body experience. And maybe in the Enlightenment or somewhere else, we divided that, and that division did great injury to how we understand ourselves, because it allowed— Akhtar: It created the modern world. Brooks: It did do that. Akhtar: We could go back to Descartes and say Descartes had a similar night of not being able to sleep and then decided to create this world that we now live in. And so there’s obviously been benefits, but we’ve lost a lot by not allowing that kind of knowledge, which again, is what I’m trying to focus on. It’s a knowledge that—I don’t know what it means. I just know that I’m experiencing it. Brooks: There’s a lot of love in the book, which I liked, and one of the most interesting relationships in the book is for the narrator with this woman, Lucy, who was the University of Chicago—lady we’ve been talking about. Akhtar: Who becomes a professor later. Brooks: And it’s literally Platonic love. So describe that love he has for her. Because he is pursuing her and fascinated by her and amazed by her, and she, by the way, has a wonderful marriage, which he does not wanna interfere with. Akhtar: I’ve had some extraordinary mentors in my life, and a number of the most important mentors have been women and have taught me about so much. And I resonate particularly—as we said earlier, there’s a lot of Plato in the book, and there’s a lot of Phaedrus in the book, one of the dialogues. And something else that there’s a lot of which I don’t talk about is the Symposium . In the Symposium , Socrates tells a story about how he learned about love and that there was an older woman who mentored him named Diotima. So Lucy’s a bit of that kind of a figure. Somebody who really has an understanding of eros in the higher sense of the word. What would it mean to relate to eros not out of a desire to possess, but to be animated by the aliveness in knowledge? So anyway, very high-minded, but I try to give it some juice in the book. David Brooks: C. S. Lewis, in his book The Four Loves , makes the distinction between “Need-love” and “Gift-love,” and Need-love proceeds out of a void, and it’s the desire to possess, to control. And Gift-love just flows out of a blessing. Akhtar: In Plato, this proposition in the Symposium is basically that love has a ladder, that you learn love in one form, and if you’re open to it, it leads to another kind of love, which then leads to another kind of love. It maybe starts with the body, but it elevates out of the body into some place higher. So, similarly, the book is exploring the possibility of what it would mean in a secular age to be related to your own experience and the experience of the world, not through a kind of materialist separation or wanting to accomplish or desire, but really just being attentive to the aliveness of that experience. Brooks: Now I’m presuming, and it’s really through your writing, you’ve had these numinous experiences. Have you had transcendent mountaintop experiences that William James used to write about, or that sort of thing? Akhtar: As time has gone on, over 30 years of various kinds of investigation and practice, I’ve had lots of different experiences. And I think more and more the experience that’s the most valuable to me is a kind of continuity of connectedness in the everyday, and feels to me more and more a better definition of the transcendent than some of the wild, dynamic, knock-your-socks-off experiences that I may have had, and that the narrator certainly does have in the book. Brooks: So connected to experience, that’s like, I am in the world . Akhtar: Connected to the continuity. There’s a continuity between us. Continuity with my ancestors. All of that stuff. That it’s here, it’s with us now. So being connected to that in a lived sense without self-consciousness That to me feels like a better definition of the transcendent. Brooks: I get that. Way before I had any faith, I had this sense of what you might call historical ecstasy. The moment of touching something or being someplace, like Chartres Cathedral or Gettysburg Battlefield, where the procession of people who’ve been there has left a residue. I was once at a home that was purported to be the home of Mary, outside of Ephesus in Turkey. I don’t know if Mary ever lived there, but centuries of prayers and mourners move through that space, and something is emanating from it, a sensation of the procession. I don’t know if I’m correctly interpreting what you’re describing. Akhtar: That’s certainly a version of what I’m talking about. I think what I’m talking about is even more prosaic. But yes. And by the way, the book does end in Chartres, interestingly. Brooks: I noticed that. Now, you have quoted Thomas Merton, and people like that, Augustine. Meister Eckhart comes up. A lot of your spiritual companions or guides, they took this, and they took it to religion. You accompany them part of the way, but you don’t take it to where they took it, which was the Bible or the Quran. Now, is that just: “I just don’t feel that. It just doesn’t feel authentic to me,” or have there been advantages and disadvantages to this spiritual sense that’s not tied to an institutionalized religion? Ayad Akhtar: It’s such a beautiful and cutting question. I don’t know. I think I’m trying to live by an empirical ethic, an ethos of being attentive to my experience, being attentive to those who’ve written about their experiences, trying to accumulate whatever wisdom over time that I can, recognizing that they are making connections both which I value and others which I don’t understand. I don’t wanna take anything on faith because to me, faith is not about an object. It’s about an orientation. I think I put it in The Atlantic essay—it is a living form of relationship with the unknown. That feels like its own worthy form of knowledge, to be in living relationship to the unknown. And not for it to have a name, because the name can sometimes get in the way of the practice. Doctrines are often things that were once practices that have now been turned into meanings. Now we consume them as meanings, but we have lost connection to the practice that led to some experience. I think mystics in general are focused on experience. And so maybe I just share that kind of granular phenomenological interest in experience itself. And I’m much more interested in that than I am in what it means. Because I’m not gonna get any kind of clarity about what it means. I may get clarity in a moment. But as the brain scans of nuns and Tibetan monks tell us—they are having very similar brain scans, but the language they use to report what their experience is is almost opposing: “union with Christ” or “emptiness.” So what does it matter what the concept is unless the concept is helping to activate technically? Does that make sense? Brooks: It does. And I’m not judging here or comparing. We’ve had two different experiences of this. Akhtar: Yours might be better. When I said it was a cutting question, I think that what my orientation lacks, which is important, is community. Because I’m a renegade out there on my own. I’ve never really talked much about this stuff. I’ve alluded to it a couple of times in interviews, but I’ve kept to myself about it, because it’s been an investigatory thing. It’s my pursuit. So I don’t have it to share with other people, which maybe suits me fine as a writer and as an observer and as an outsider, and maybe that’s my life choice, but I think it does deprive me of community. Brooks: Shiva, say, the Jewish mourning ritual, is a beautiful, very spiritually and intellectually very sophisticated way to handle grief. It also gives everybody in the congregation—they know what to do. Everyone knows exactly what to do. And I would say religion has provided me with a broader sensation, at least the way I process spiritual experiences. I was having one of these numinous experiences in Colorado. I was on the top of a mountain by a lake. And because I’m me—and even I was not a big believer then, I was still wandering in those days—I brought up a book called The Valley of Vision , which is a collection of Puritan prayers. I happened to open it when I’m having this very moving and beautiful experience. And the first prayer is a very famous one: “Lord, high and holy, meek and lowly, thou hast brought me to the valley of vision, where I live in the depths and see thee in the heights. Hemmed in by mountains of sin, I behold thy glory. Let me learn by paradox, the way down is the way up. To be low is to be high. To be brokenhearted is to be a healed heart. A contrite spirit is a rejoicing spirit. A repenting soul is the victorious soul.” And when I read that, it’s really a prayer of the beatitudinal wisdom. All these spiritual inversions. It gave me something to hold on to. And it also gave me a sense, which I remember thinking, that there is a moral order to the universe. I had a sense of this moral order before I had a sense of God, that this is so beautiful, these inversions. And there’s a structure to them, and it’s sort of an intellectual encompassing of everything that I love. I have a friend named David Wolpe who was a rabbi in L.A. He’s retired since. He had a passage which has rung in my mind, which I wanted to read to you to get your reaction. And he does not believe in “spiritual without religious.” And he writes this: “Spirituality is an emotion. Religion is an obligation. Spirituality soothes. Religion mobilizes. Spirituality is satisfied with itself. Religion is dissatisfied with the world.” Akhtar: I think my book is a direct contradiction of that orientation. I respect that quote a lot, and I think that it’s largely true, but it’s also clearly not. I’m interested by this idea that you’re at the top of the mountain and you’re having an experience, and in that moment you reach for language. I don’t. That’s the difference. And I don’t know what value that difference has for other people. I know that for me, reaching for language in that moment fixes the experience. And I want the experience to continue to exhibit that continuity that I was talking about earlier. That’s a technical matter, actually. By allowing it to be, it is allowed to have a different evolution. That’s just something that I’ve learned, that the meaning I could derive from the experience is ultimately less lasting and less valuable than continuing to relate to the experience. Brooks: But someone in your book says to the character, “You’re seeking states, not truth.” Now, when you’re talking about not reducing it to language, how do you retain it? Akhtar: The aspirant who hates God only has to be around for three more lifetimes. If you focus on it, you’re gonna retain something. Language is not a way to retain it. Language is a way to no longer relate to it. In my experience. So that’s why the challenge of the book was how to articulate this experience in a language. Between my last book and this book, I learned something about the sentence. Sentences for me before this book were about a meaning conveyed between punctuation. In this book, somehow the sentence became a way to move inquiry and energy across punctuation into the next sentence. And so it was like, in a way—like the scene with Bloom, what is the force that’s moving? There’s a movement that once it begins shouldn’t stop, and it should not be stopped by any meaning. It should not be stopped by any scene. There has to be some absorbing continuity that the reader is drawn into. Brooks: That gets me back to my friend Gregory of Nyssa. He’s about spiritual movement. I once read a book by a guy named John Coates, who’s a neuroscientist, who said, We didn’t evolve to solve problems. We evolved to move across a landscape . And he says, If you think of the brain as an organ designed to foster movement, you will never see yourself the same way again . And that’s true: Since I read that sentence, I’ve never seen it the same. Akhtar: And that’s what happened to me with the sentence, the writing of a sentence, understanding how a sentence could function with this book. That it functioned to move, not to fix. Brooks: Now, there’s a moment, and I keep ruining our conversation with neuroscience, but— Akhtar: There’s a lot of neuroscience in the book. Brooks: I know. That’s what I’m getting to. There’s a scene where the character’s like, What is going on in my brain that all this is happening? So he goes to a doctor. He says, Oh, your insula —which is a part of the brain— it’s growing . Akhtar: Thickened. Brooks: Now, should I see that scene as a de-sacralization of his experience, of his condition? I was somehow disappointed. He’s reducing it to the insula? And I’ve been guilty in the last conversation to do that, but— Akhtar: We all are. I think when the medical vocabulary enters our experience, it becomes the final vocabulary. It is our way of materializing that immaterial terror of death that we have. Because we’re so frightened of death, rightly so—or as Montaigne would say, not rightly so—that medical language, which is the primary language of mortality, and morality on some level in our culture becomes the final way to talk about anything. So it was impossible to write this book without including the medical map, without including the medical language. It’s been demonstrated that activation of this area of the insula that’s up against the temporal lobe creates religious experience. So what are the implications of that? What are the implications of there being a physiological corollary to the experience that the narrator’s having? Does it disqualify that experience? There’s lots of instances of the uncanny in the book as well. So that presumably is not explained by the brain scans, and yet all those things have to coexist because those are the languages of the 21st century. I didn’t wanna write a book that was not responsible to the languages that we live in. I wanted to write a book that at least attempted a process of restoring a magic—at least for me as a writer as I was writing it—of the inner life, because it felt to me that that was something that we’re all more and more sensitive to and longing for. David Brooks: C. S. Lewis, before he was—alongside of being the writer of the Narnia stories, he was a medievalist. He wrote about medieval literature. He said something was lost when humans used to look up to the night sky and they would see magic, enchanted. Now we see balls of gas burning that lie far away. Akhtar: That’s the opening quote of my book, by the way. György Lukács. There was a time when we would look up at the starry skies and see the map of all possibilities. Brooks: Have we lost something, or is there something we need to be on the watch out for as our culture has trended in this direction? Akhtar: I don’t know. I know that I don’t wanna lose it. And so my focus is not losing it. I focus as much as possible on that invisible, immaterial inner part of us that is the substance of our moral life. The Russians wrote about it beautifully. It’s why we still read the Russians. I don’t know why we got so timid writing about such things. So yeah, I think we certainly have lost something, but I don’t wanna lose it. Brooks: I do think that’s why I read the Russians too. That moment when, say, in Tolstoy, Prince Andrei is on the battlefield somewhere and he looks up at the endless vastness of the sky, or Levin is cutting grass and he has this experience of— Akhtar: Or Ivan Ilyich at the end is consumed and subsumed by a radiance. Brooks: And they’re not all happy people. They had the radiance, and they— Akhtar: I don’t think a fundamental orientation in soulfulness is about happiness. I think that the great saints and in all the traditions—and in your own tradition, Christ, he’s not happy. The lesson is not happiness. And I feel like that is part of the problem of our orientation to some of this stuff. Brooks: He could’ve been like, “Six life hacks to be a happy Messiah.” Akhtar: Happiness is overrated. Happiness of a certain ilk, I think, is overrated if you really wanna talk about this kind of stuff. Brooks: I would say some of the things that challenge my spiritual life are my achievement orientation, time orientation. There’s a lot you have to let go of, which I have trouble doing. You mentioned earlier—maybe we’ll close on this, because it’s a fascinating part of the novel and your own life that I can’t explain and don’t understand, which is you talked about your dreams and these coincidences that you often dream. Describe some of that and what it means to you. Akhtar: I still don’t understand it. I started keeping track of my dreams in college and then really accelerated that sort of focus on my nightlife, if you will, between the ages of 22 and 26 when I was sleeping with a pencil tied to my finger to remind me when I would get into that hypnagogic state that there was something I needed to write down. So I’d write down every dream. And during this period, one thing that started to happen with a degree of unpredictable regularity was that I would dream of something that seemed to then happen. I talk about it a little bit in The Atlantic essay, and it’s usually pretty prosaic stuff, but still didn’t make any sense why this would happen, and seemed to point to the fact that maybe space-time was not what we think it is. Even if I had no other way of knowing that. This has recurred throughout my life, as I’ve continued to pay attention to my dreams. Unfortunately, I’ve never seen any lottery numbers. So I don’t know what it means, but it clearly is a mystery and does point to there maybe being more in heaven and Earth than is contained in the kinds of books that I, and all of us, tend to read. That’s part of the novel as well. The psychoanalytic tradition does deal with this a bit because it’s a phenomenon that occurs relatively regularly within analytic settings at times. They have some sort of way of working with it, but it’s interesting. I don’t know what it means. I’m not sure what the utility of this strange proclivity that I’ve had, but I know that it’s a fact. It’s a subjective fact that I have to deal with. And it must tell me something about the world that I’m living in, which is different in essence than how it appears. Brooks: I hope people have listened to us and got a sense of how valuable and important this book is. I really mean that, because sometimes we’re feeling we’re fighting the shallowification of life. Maybe you would call it the rationalization, or Max Weber, the iron cage, or we’re now in a silicon cage. And to delve into these regions strikes me as the most important thing we can do to preserve our humanity. It’s not always easy, and it’s not always clear, but it’s where our efforts should be, and people should definitely buy this book. I don’t know if you have any closing thoughts. Ayad Akhtar: I’m just grateful, David. I’m so gratified to have this conversation with you, and I think the name of your new endeavor here, The Permanent Questions , is beautiful and right on. Brooks: One of the highlights for me of my conversation with Ayad is when he pushed back on the David Wolpe quote I read, criticizing people who are spiritual and not religious. He is spiritual and not religious, and I have to say he is more spiritually evolved certainly than me and maybe more than a lot of pastors I know. He has put in the work, done the reading from Plato to Meister Eckhart to Thomas Merton, and he’s constructed a spiritual sense. And it’s humbling to see that. The thing I 100 percent agree with him on is that we do our culture harm when we try to bleach spiritual talk out of our public conversation, public debate. Human beings, religious or not religious, are metaphysical creatures, and if you take that element out of our lives and out of our common lives, you’re doing real damage to your society and to the people in it. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Ayad Akhtar. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic in partnership with Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you wanna support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. See you next week.

item.title: Community concerned for safety as search for sexually violent predator continues
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The news of Merle Wakefield escape has reignited concerns among this Rancho Bernardo community who once fought very hard to keep a sexual violent predator from being placed in this neighborhood. “It’s a little bit creepy and unsettling for sure,” Jeff Grace said. Jeff is among many Rancho Bernardo neighbors keeping their head on a swivel for Mere Wakefield. Wakefield is convicted of lewd acts on a child in 1980 and rape by means of force, violence, or fear in 1991. In 2021, Jeff led the Keep Rancho Berardo Safe Movement against Douglas Badger, another sexual violent predator that was going to be placed in their community. “We have a lot unanswered questions much like we did in 2021 when the state wanted to put badger in Rancho Bernardo,” Jeff Grace said. Since Badger’s case, Jeff has kept a close eye on sexually violent predators to ensure they are not placed in his neighborhood. Jeff said on July 7, 2024, Liberty Health Care planned to place Wakefield at home on Sycamore Canyon Road. Five days later, he and other community members rallied against that placement. That same day, the DA’s office notified them Liberty Health Care was no longer moving forward with that plan. “It made us feel great, and it took these residents that lived in this kind of one-way-in, one-way-out garden road community, they went from pure fear to tears of joy,” Jeff Grace said. The peace of mind was short-lived. After serving several years in prison and in the state mental hospital, in November of that year, Wakefield was placed on transient release. At last check, he was being temporarily housed at 1138 Custer Road in Campo. “When he was placed on transient release, nobody really knew where he was going to be. In fact, the judge when putting him on status said she was okay with putting him in an RV,” Grace said. On Friday, investigators under Liberty Health Care’s 24 hour supervision said Wakefield walked off from the job at the Amazon Processing Center in Rancho Bernardo. Sheriff investigators said he cut his monitor around 3:30 a.m. Friday. A law enforcement source said Wakefield threw his cell phone into the bushes then drove away in his 2018 White Toyota Camry. “This is the first time that something this dramatic has happened,” Jeff Grace said. Jeff said he is doing what he can to keep his community safe and he hopes others do the same. “The most immediate concern is keep your eye on your kids and keep your doors locked, I mean, that’s all we can do,” Grace said. NBC 7 got in touch with an Amazon spokesperson who shared the following statement, “We are looking into this incident and gathering additional information. We are in contact with law enforcement and will defer to them for any details about the investigation.” This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

item.title: Colombian paramilitary group leader extradited to San Diego
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The leader of a Colombian paramilitary organization that allegedly dealt in cocaine cultivation and production was extradited to San Diego Friday, where he faces federal charges that include narco-terrorism and conspiracy to distribute cocaine. Geovany Andres Rojas, 45, also known as Araña, led Comandos de la Frontera, an organization that exerted control over one of Colombia’s top cocaine producing regions, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. The group was made up of ex-combatants from Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia, which signed a peace accord with Colombia’s president in 2016, though smaller FARC factions continued engaging in armed conflicts. The U.S. Attorney’s Office alleges Rojas was a member of FARC when the peace agreement was signed, but later rejected it, resumed armed activities, and became a guerilla leader. Colombian officials handed Rojas off to U.S. law enforcement officials Friday morning and he arrived in San Diego late Friday afternoon, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said. Rojas is due to make his initial court appearance in San Diego on Monday afternoon.

According to the city of Encinitas, it was made aware that a portion of the bluff Grandview Beach, just north of the staircase, collapsed on Sept. 18. Earlier this year, a nearly $1-million project refurbished the stairs, but after the most recent collapse, they closed again, catching locals and visitors by surprise Friday. “It’s my first time coming and actually seeing the fence all locked up,” Jason Parks, an Encinitas resident, said Similar reactions were echoed by others trying to take in the ocean view from the Grandview Stairs. “I understand why the city is doing it, but kind of a bummer. But you know, gotta be concerned for the residents,” Parks said. “I understand why.” The area is a premier coastal entry point for sightseers and surfers, but it’s now blocked by a chain-link fence. “Oh, I’m disappointed,” Dough Barkett, a local surfer, said. After engineers inspected the crumbled side of the coast, there’s concern additional bluff failure could happen again within 300 feet, north and south, of the staircase. The city says California State Parks is responsible for the north side, while they cover the south side. In a statement to NBC7, a spokesperson from California State Parks advised anyone visiting state beaches should time visits at low tide when there is more sand between the cliffs and waves to maintain a safe distance from the bluffs. “I think closing the access to the surfers only inhibits our ability to do what we enjoy doing and I think the chances are slim of something happening that I think it’s an overreaction,” Barkett said. San Diego State University Geology Professor Emeritus Dr. Pat Abbott says he’s recorded five sea collapses that have resulted in one or more deaths, including the 2019 bluff collapse at Grandview Beach that killed three people. “When you look at that beach cliff from where we are at, the stairs looking northward along there, you can just see this nicely cleaned off area where the 2019 fall area is now adjoining the one that just happened to make one long, continuous cliff,” Abbott said. After an active summer of warmer-than-normal-sea-surface temperatures and elevated surf, plus with bigger waves on the way this weekend , Abbott calls the conditions primed for what could be an eventful fall and winter, which could impact coastal erosion. And although he says these collapses are unpredictable, they will happen again, he says. “Ultimately, we’re going to get surprises like we just had a few days ago,” Abbott said. While the city continues to monitor the beach, they say access to the coast from the Grandview Stairs will be closed for an unknown amount of time, but they ask visitors to avoid the area. Beach access is still available at Beacons Beach and Ponto Beach.

item.title: Meta's new motto: we care about privacy
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Meta is seeking to make privacy protections a centerpiece of new products including its viral assistant Muse , marking a major shift for a company built on extensive use of customer data. Why it matters: The radical turnaround is an acknowledgment that the winner of AI's new assistant race will have to reassure users that they can turn over their emails, finances, health data and other sensitive information. Without that, a super-intelligent personal agent is essentially useless. Driving the news: Meta, whose privacy policy once allowed it nearly unfettered access to use almost everything people did with Meta AI (in almost any way it wanted), has made a significant shift in recent months to put privacy at the center of its AI strategy. In a 6,500-word August manifesto , CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a broad promise. " We believe that people should have a fully private mode for personal agents where even Meta or any other service provider cannot see or grant access to your information." With Muse, which appears to be on a path to becoming one of the most popular AI hits since ChatGPT, the company is offering all customers their own personal virtual machine. A soon-to-be-available option would ensure that even Meta won't have access to the data. Meta is also readying a similar "private processing" option for interactions with its AI glasses. Small efforts have been underway for more than a year, starting with the addition of incognito chats and private processing , which arrived first in WhatsApp, where Meta also provides end-to-end encryption. More recently, the options have spread to other Meta apps. Yes, but: Customers still have to pay close attention if they want to minimize the amount of data shared with Meta. In Muse, for example, the default setting allows interactions to be used for training the company's AI models, though that can be turned off. And not all of the privacy changes being offered to Muse users apply to those accessing Meta AI in other ways, such as through the Facebook, Instagram or Meta AI apps. Plus, Meta devices continue to spur other types of privacy concerns. "Meta's products that embed microphones and cameras in everyday devices pose serious privacy risks to people just trying to live their lives and go about their day without being recorded or surveilled," Electronic Privacy Information Center executive director Alan Butler told Axios. "Confidential processing doesn't solve the problem of pushing embedded surveillance systems out into the world." The big picture: Meta has spent years building a thriving business based on tapping extensive knowledge about its customers to serve up content and ads that it knows will be right up their alley. Its practices have also drawn lawsuits from a wide range of entities that say Meta designed social media to be addictive and caused harm. How it works: Meta is betting on a new business model to fund Muse, which won't provide the same data for targeted advertising that supports most of the company's services. Muse has $20- and $100-per-month paid tiers for heavy users, but Meta expects the free tier to account for most usage. "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," Zuckerberg said. Our thought bubble : There's still a trust gap based on Meta's years of gobbling up nearly all the data it could. That can't be addressed with words, but requires establishing a new track record.
